title: Your long discourse
hook: of the long discourses, which one stays with you

segments.voice: Yesterday: by tens, Sariputta's grid of ten questions. Your line: what helps, what to let go. Today, the end of a week, and a question only you can answer.

Ask ten people who read the same novel what they remember, and you'll get ten different scenes. One remembers the storm. One, a line at a kitchen table. One, a side character nobody else noticed. Nine of them didn't read it wrong. A long book is a house with many rooms, and each reader ends up living in one. For seven weeks, this path has walked through the thirty-four Long Discourses. Kings, gods, wanderers, a courtesan, a skeptic prince, a young man bowing to the sky. Today adds nothing new.
screen: `TEN READERS, TEN SCENES.` → `A HOUSE WITH MANY ROOMS.` → `WHICH ROOM DO YOU LIVE IN?`

segments.voice: Some scenes, in case one is waiting for you. A king who killed his own father rides out under a full moon, asking what a spiritual life is good for, and hears that even a slave who goes forth would be honored by a king. A man builds a staircase to a palace he has never seen. A woman named Ambapali invites the Buddha to a meal, and when princes ask for the same day, he keeps his word to her. The Buddha, old and ill, tells Ananda there's no teacher's closed fist: nothing held back. Ananda weeps by a door, and the Buddha praises his long kindness as an attendant. A skeptical prince argues with a monk through story after story. And this week: young Sigala, bowing to six directions, learns what each bow could mean. Six ways wealth leaks away. How to tell a true friend. Duties that run both ways, between parents and children, teachers and students, spouses, friends, workers. Then Sariputta, counting so nothing is lost, and counting again by tens. In the last journey, the Buddha says that after he's gone, the teaching and the discipline will be the teacher. Not a person, not a successor: the words. And words do their work by being remembered. So the scene that stays with you isn't trivia. It's the teacher you actually took home, and it doesn't have to match anyone else's.
screen: `A MOONLIT KING, A STAIRCASE, A MEAL` · `THIS WEEK: SIGALA'S SIX DIRECTIONS` · `THE TEACHING WILL BE YOUR TEACHER` · `THE SCENE THAT STAYED IS YOURS` · then, large: `YOURS.`

segments.voice: Let one scene from these weeks come up on its own, whichever arrives first, and walk into it slowly: where is it, what time of day, who is speaking, what does the air feel like? Stay inside it for a few breaths, the way you'd stand in a room you love. Then notice why this one came, without explaining it, and rest.
Digha Nikaya, the long collection: the one scene, out of thirty-four discourses, that stayed with you, the teaching you actually carried home. Today's word.
Your line: yours. One scene, carried home with you. A week done, day five hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Individual long discourses, such as the account of the Buddha's last days or the advice to Sigala, are read, chanted and taught on their own in Buddhist communities.

original.note: Pali Digha Nikaya: the long collection, thirty-four discourses.

trapdoor: what you thought: the long discourses are one long book you either know or don't.
what it means: they're thirty-four separate scenes and teachings, and different readers carry different ones home.
what a scholar hears: the Digha Nikaya is grouped in three books, and individual discourses like DN 16 and DN 31 have long histories of being taught and copied on their own.

chat.says: You read all thirty-four long Buddhist discourses? Which scene matters most?
options: The one that stays with you; the teaching itself is meant to be the teacher.
Only the first one; the rest just repeat it at greater length.
The longest one, since length shows which teaching mattered most.
chat.meaning: In DN 16 the Buddha says the teaching and discipline will be the teacher; the scene you remember is the teaching you carried home.

Ambapali.meaning: a courtesan who invited the Buddha to a meal

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's cousin and longtime attendant

Sigala.meaning: a young householder who bowed to six directions

Sariputta.meaning: the Buddha's senior student, known for wisdom

Digha Nikaya.meaning: the long collection: thirty-four long discourses

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta: the teaching and discipline as teacher
